planting.note: Set divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Lavender Vista is a widely sold tetraploid known for reliable performance across a wide range of climates.

directions: Lavender Vista carries round, lightly fragrant lavender flowers with a crisp white midrib and a wide yellow-green throat, held on sturdy scapes above semi-evergreen foliage. Bloom begins early in the season and the clump reblooms through summer, giving a longer flowering window than many older lavender-toned daylilies. It thrives in average garden soil with regular moisture and benefits from division every three to four years to keep the fan count vigorous and flowering heavy. Deadheading spent blooms keeps the scapes tidy but is not required for continued bud production.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, moist but well-drained loam in full sun to part sun; this 1996 Salter-hybridized tetraploid cultivar went on to earn an American Hemerocallis Society Award of Merit.

directions: Awesome Blossom opens large, five-inch antique-rose to apricot flowers overlaid with a distinctive raisin-plum eyezone and a lime-green throat, a color combination that stands out among early-midseason daylilies. Each flower lasts only a single day, but the evergreen clump pushes new scapes from early into late summer, making it one of the more dependable rebloomers for extending the daylily season. It performs best in fertile, evenly moist soil and, like most evergreen types, benefits from winter mulch protection in its colder hardiness range. Established clumps spread slowly by rhizome and rarely need dividing more than once every few years.

planting.note: Set dormant-type divisions in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun; My Melinda was hybridized by Warner, registered in 1984, and received an American Hemerocallis Society Honorable Mention in 1990 for its clean color and extended bloom.

directions: My Melinda bears clear pink self-colored flowers about three and a half inches across with a contrasting green throat, carried on scapes to roughly two feet tall. It is a mid-season rebloomer with an extended bloom habit, meaning well-established clumps can throw additional scapes well past the main early-summer flush. As a dormant-foliage type it goes fully leafless in winter and is reliably hardy into colder zones without special protection. Routine division every three to four years keeps clumps floriferous and prevents overcrowding.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring with the crown set a couple of inches deep and roots shaded from direct sun; raised by Charles Noble around 1881 and named for the British prime minister, this is one of the oldest large-flowered clematis still widely offered.

directions: W.E. Gladstone produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, pale lavender to light blue blooms of six to eight tepals that can reach ten inches or more across, opening from early summer into early autumn. Because it flowers on both old and new wood, it needs only light pruning in early spring just above the lowest healthy buds rather than a hard cutback. Give it a sturdy support to climb, since mature vines can reach well over eight feet, and keep the root zone cool and mulched while the top growth enjoys full sun. Its flower size and long bloom season have kept it in cultivation for well over a century.

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level; introduced in the United Kingdom around 1990, Sealand Gem is a large-flowered cultivar compact enough for containers and small trellises.

directions: Sealand Gem opens semi-double, rosy-mauve flowers shaded with lilac and marked by a darker pink central star, blooming from June into September on a vigorous but manageable vine. Its relatively restrained habit compared with other large-flowered hybrids makes it a good choice for growing against a pergola post or in a large container on a patio. It tolerates a range of soils from clay to sandy loam as long as drainage is reasonable and moisture is kept consistent through the growing season. Light pruning in early spring, removing dead or weak growth above a strong bud, keeps the vine tidy without sacrificing its early flush of bloom.

planting.note: Plant in spring in rich, well-drained soil with the crown set a few inches deep; this Clematis texensis selection was raised in France and introduced in 1918, named by its breeder in memory of a son lost in the First World War.

directions: This texensis-type clematis bears lightly scented, tulip-shaped flowers in strawberry-pink bars over a creamy white background, smaller and more textured than large-flowered hybrids but produced in flushes through May, June, and again in September. Being a herbaceous-stemmed type that dies back to the base each winter, it is cut hard to the ground in late winter or early spring along with the rest of the previous year's growth, after which all bloom is produced on fresh new vines. It does well scrambling through a shrub, up a narrow trellis, or trailing from a large container, and prefers consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil. Its compact root system and modest two-to-three-foot spread make it well suited to smaller gardens than many other clematis.
